We are seeing occasional connection pool exhaustion on our FastAPI service during morning traffic spikes. How should we tune SQLAlchemy async pool settings, connection recycling, and health checks?

[Session 1 Engineering Notes - FastAPI async database pooling]
When tuning an async SQLAlchemy engine under high concurrency, start by separating steady-state pool size from burst capacity. Set pool_size=20 and max_overflow=10 per worker process, keeping total connections across all Uvicorn workers safely below PostgreSQL max_connections (ideally leaving 20% headroom for migrations and monitoring). Enable pool_pre_ping=True to validate stale TCP sockets before checkout, and configure pool_recycle=1800 so connections rotate before idle firewall or NAT timeouts drop them silently. Avoid holding database sessions open across external HTTP calls: fetch the required rows, commit or close the session immediately, perform outbound API calls, and open a short-lived transaction only when persisting the response. Add a lightweight SELECT 1 readiness check on /readyz separate from /healthz so orchestrators stop routing traffic before pool exhaustion cascades into 504 gateway timeouts. Finally, track checkout wait latency via SQLAlchemy pool events (checkout and checkin hooks) and alert when p95 wait exceeds 50 ms.

Our Docker image for the Python microservice has grown to 1.4 GB and CI builds take 9 minutes. Can you walk through a clean multi-stage Dockerfile and layer caching strategy?

[Session 1 Engineering Notes - Docker multi-stage Python builds]
A 1.4 GB Python image usually happens when build-essential, gcc, git, and pip wheel caches remain in the final runtime layer. Switch to a two-stage build based on python:3.12-slim. In the builder stage, install compilers only if needed, create a dedicated virtual environment at /opt/venv, and copy only pyproject.toml and lockfiles before running pip install so dependency layers stay cached unless requirements change. In the final runtime stage, copy /opt/venv from the builder, add a non-root appuser, set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 and PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, and copy application source last. A reporting query filtering on tenant_id, created_at range, and a JSONB tags column is doing sequential scans on 12 million rows. How should we index and verify the execution plan?

[Session 1 Engineering Notes - PostgreSQL B-tree vs GIN indexing]
Composite B-tree indexes and GIN indexes solve different predicates, so examine selectivity with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) first. If tenant_id plus the created_at range already narrows the candidate set to a few thousand rows, a composite B-tree index on (tenant_id, created_at DESC) will satisfy the equality and range predicates cleanly, and PostgreSQL can filter the remaining JSONB tags in memory with low shared buffer reads. Conversely, if individual tenants have millions of rows and queries filter heavily on JSONB containment (@>), create a dedicated GIN index using jsonb_path_ops on the tags column, or combine btree_gin if tenant_id must participate in a single bitmap index scan. Always test with realistic parameter values because bind-parameter skew can cause the planner to prefer a sequential scan on large tenants. Avoid indexing low-cardinality booleans standalone; use partial indexes (WHERE archived = false) when 95% of queries target active records.

Someone merged a regression into main sometime in the last 40 commits while refactoring request validation. What is the cleanest git bisect and fixup workflow without rewriting shared main history?

[Session 1 Engineering Notes - Git interactive rebase and bisect workflow]
Never rewrite commits that have already been pushed to shared main. Start by checking out a clean branch or detached worktree and running git bisect start HEAD <last_known_good_sha>. If you have a reproducible pytest case (for example pytest tests/test_validation.py -k test_payload), automate the entire search with git bisect run pytest tests/test_validation.py -k test_payload. Git will perform a binary search across the 40 commits in about 6 steps and print the exact offending commit hash. Run git bisect reset immediately afterward so your working tree returns to normal. Create a fresh fix branch from origin/main, apply the surgical fix alongside a regression test, and open a pull request referencing the offending commit. For your own unpushed feature branches, git commit --fixup <sha> paired with git rebase -i --autosquash keeps PR commits tidy.

During rolling deployments in Kubernetes, we observe a brief burst of 502 errors for in-flight requests. Why does this happen and how do preStop hooks and terminationGracePeriodSeconds fix it?

[Session 2 Engineering Notes - Kubernetes readiness probes and graceful shutdown]
Brief 502 bursts during rolling updates occur because EndpointSlice propagation to kube-proxy and ingress controllers happens asynchronously in parallel with SIGTERM delivery to the pod. If Uvicorn or Gunicorn stops accepting connections or exits immediately on SIGTERM, the ingress still routes new requests to a closing socket for 2 to 5 seconds. Fix this in three places: first, add a lifecycle preStop exec hook running sleep 5 so the container stays alive while endpoints drain from load balancers. Second, configure your application server graceful shutdown timeout to exceed the longest legitimate request duration (for instance 25 seconds), and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40 on the Pod spec so Kubernetes does not send SIGKILL prematurely. Third, ensure readinessProbe fails fast when shutdown begins by flipping an internal draining flag on SIGTERM while continuing to finish already-accepted HTTP requests cleanly.

When a hot Redis cache key expires under heavy load, dozens of workers simultaneously hit the primary database. What patterns prevent cache stampedes reliably?

[Session 2 Engineering Notes - Redis cache stampede protection]
To prevent cache stampedes (dog-piling), combine TTL jitter, probabilistic early expiration, and single-flight locking. First, add random jitter (+/- 15%) to every cache TTL so keys populated during a batch warm-up do not expire simultaneously. Second, for expensive aggregations, wrap cache misses in a short-lived distributed lock (SET lock_key token NX PX 3000) or per-process asyncio.Lock keyed by cache key: only one worker recomputes the value while peers either await briefly or serve a slightly stale cached payload using stale-while-revalidate semantics (storing logical_expiry inside the JSON payload with a longer physical Redis TTL). Always release locks using an atomic Lua compare-and-delete script checking the unique owner token so a slow worker never deletes another worker's fresh lock.

In Python 3.12 asyncio, what are the subtle pitfalls with asyncio.wait_for, TaskGroup, and CancelledError when cleaning up network clients?

[Session 2 Engineering Notes - Python asyncio task cancellation and timeouts]
In Python 3.12, prefer asyncio.timeout() context managers and asyncio.TaskGroup over legacy patterns where possible. Remember that CancelledError inherits from BaseException (not Exception), so broad except Exception blocks do not swallow cancellation, which is desirable; however, if you catch BaseException or CancelledError to close sockets or flush buffers, you must always re-raise CancelledError unless you explicitly own and intend to consume the cancellation boundary. Inside async finally blocks, wrap critical cleanup coroutines with asyncio.shield only carefully—if a task is already cancelled, an unshielded await inside finally will be cancelled immediately too. Use asyncio.TaskGroup for structured concurrency so sibling tasks are cancelled and awaited deterministically when one child raises, preventing silent background task leaks and unawaited warnings.
